extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether an application/specification satisfies the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (pre-AIA 112, first paragraph), including how to assess support for claims, genus/species issues, examiner burdens, and typical circumstances that give rise to written description questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possession (written description) standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must show that the applicant was in possession of the claimed invention; the fundamental factual inquiry is whether the specification conveys with reasonable clarity to those skilled in the art that, as of the filing date sought, applicant was in possession of the invention as now claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objective standard formulations include: 'does the description clearly allow persons of ordinary skill in the art to recognize that he or she invented what is claimed' and Vas-Cath's requirement that the applicant convey with reasonable clarity that he or she was in possession of the invention. Possession may be shown using words, structures, figures, diagrams, formulas, reduction to practice, or by describing distinguishing identifying characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors to consider in possession determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the specification shows possession is a factual determination reached by considering a number of factors, including the level of skill and knowledge in the art, partial structure, physical and/or chemical properties, functional characteristics alone or coupled with a known or disclosed correlation between structure and function, and the method of making the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure of any combination of such identifying characteristics that distinguish the claimed invention from other materials and would lead one of skill in the art to conclude applicant was in possession is sufficient. Examiners should rely on patents and printed publications to determine art maturity and level of skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation by nature/scope of invention and art maturity
rubrics_metrics.description: The description needed to satisfy 35 U.S.C. 112 varies with the nature and scope of the invention at issue, and with the scientific and technological knowledge already in existence; in mature arts less evidence is required while in emerging or unpredictable technologies more evidence is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In most mature technologies, written description should not be raised for claims present when originally filed even if only a method and function are disclosed. For unpredictable arts, disclosure of only a method and function may not support a product claim; more specific characterization or corroborating evidence is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-by-process claims and process disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the process has actually been used to produce the product, the written description requirement for a product-by-process claim is clearly satisfied; however, the requirement may not be satisfied where it is not clear that the acts set forth in the specification can be performed, or that the product is produced by that process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification does not establish that the disclosed process produces the claimed product (or is operable), the written description for the product may be inadequate. Examiners should evaluate whether the process was actually used/reported and whether operability is evident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial structure disclosure insufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure of a partial structure without additional characterization of the product may not be sufficient to evidence possession of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For complex chemical/biological inventions, conception requires ability to define and distinguish the compound (structure, method of preparation, properties). Merely stating a principal biological property (e.g., 'encodes human erythropoietin') without enabling specificity is often insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus claims: representative species requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The written description requirement for a claimed genus may be satisfied through sufficient description of a representative number of species by actual reduction to practice, reduction to drawings, or by disclosure of relevant identifying characteristics sufficient to show applicant was in possession of the claimed genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'representative number of species' means the species described must be representative of the entire genus. When there is substantial variation within the genus, one must describe a sufficient variety of species to reflect that variation. If representative species are not disclosed for a genus, the genus claim must be rejected for lack of written description.

rubrics_metrics.name: When one species can or cannot support a genus
rubrics_metrics.description: The disclosure of only one species adequately describes a genus only if the disclosure 'indicates that the patentee has invented species sufficient to constitute the genus,' i.e., one skilled in the art would understand the inventor invented the genus, not merely a single species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In unpredictable arts, a single species usually will not suffice. There are exceptions where the disclosed species unambiguously shows conception of the broader genus (e.g., where the method or property makes other species obvious or irrelevant). Cases like Rasmussen and Herschler provide examples where one species sufficed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure-function correlation as basis for genus support
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification may support a genus by establishing a reasonable structure-function correlation, either by the inventor's disclosure or by what was known in the art at the time of filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such correlations allow description of a representative genus without enumerating every species. Examiners should assess whether the specification provides correlation or whether it is known in the art; absent such correlation, broader genus claims may be unsupported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative disclosure does not require per-species support
rubrics_metrics.description: Description of a representative number of species does not require specificity sufficient to provide individual support for each species in the genus; e.g., in molecular biology, disclosure of an amino acid sequence can support nucleic acid genus claims because the genetic code is widely known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the technical knowledge (like the genetic code) makes certain direct derivations routine; where common scientific knowledge bridges descriptions, broader claims can be supported without explicit per-species disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Each claim limitation must be supported in original disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: To comply with the written description requirement or to be entitled to an earlier priority/filing date, each claim limitation must be expressly, implicitly, or inherently supported in the originally filed disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an explicit limitation in a claim is not present in the written description whose benefit is sought, it must be shown that a person of ordinary skill would have understood that the description requires that limitation (Hyatt v. Boone). Examiners should evaluate express, implicit, and inherent support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner initial burden in written description rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: A description as filed is presumed adequate unless or until the examiner presents sufficient evidence or reasoning to rebut the presumption; the examiner has the initial burden of presenting by a preponderance of evidence why a person skilled in the art would not recognize in the disclosure the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner must set forth express findings of fact supporting lack of written description and should not rely on conclusory allegations. See Wertheim; the examiner's role is to establish a reasonable basis for challenge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required express findings when rejecting for lack of written description
rubrics_metrics.description: When rejecting a claim for lack of written description the examiner's findings should: (A) identify the claim limitation at issue; and (B) establish a prima facie case by providing reasons why a person skilled in the art at the time would not have recognized that the inventor was in possession of the invention as claimed in view of the original disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A general allegation such as 'unpredictability in the art' is not sufficient. Findings should be factual and tied to the disclosure and the knowledge in the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on adding new matter and treatment of amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim is amended to include subject matter, limitations, or terminology not present in the application as filed, involving a departure from, addition to, or deletion from the disclosure, the examiner should conclude the claimed subject matter is not described in that application and reject under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or deny priority/benefit as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While the analysis for new matter and written description is similar, the procedural treatment differs. Applicant should specifically point out support for amendments and examiners should be mindful of new matter rules (MPEP § 714.02, § 2163.06).

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling applicant replies to written description rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon reply by applicant, the examiner must reassess the patentability of the claimed invention, including whether the written description requirement is now satisfied, by reperforming the analysis in view of the whole record (amendments, arguments, evidence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the whole record demonstrates adequacy, the examiner should not repeat the rejection. If inadequacy remains, the examiner should fully respond to applicant's rebuttal, properly treat further showings, and thoroughly analyze any affidavits relevant to written description (In re Alton).

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential/critical elements must be claimed
rubrics_metrics.description: Each claim must include all elements which the applicant has described as essential; if an element described as essential is not claimed, the claim may be rejected as lacking adequate written description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases like Johnson Worldwide and Gentry Gallery illustrate that omission of described essential elements can undermine claim support; examiners should identify such essential elements from the disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical circumstances giving rise to written description issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Written description issues typically arise in: (I) amendments affecting a claim; (II) reliance on filing date of a parent application under 35 U.S.C. 120; (III) reliance on priority under 35 U.S.C. 119; (IV) support for a claim corresponding to a count in an interference; and (V) when an original claim is not sufficiently described (functional-only definitions or broad genus vs narrow species).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should consult MPEP § 2163 for guidelines and relevant case law for each circumstance (e.g., Tronzo, Ziegler, Gosteli). In interferences or priority claims, the earlier application must meet 112(a) for the subject matter relied upon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherency standards for implied support
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish inherency, extrinsic evidence must make clear that the missing descriptive matter is necessarily present in the thing described and would be recognized by persons of ordinary skill; inherency cannot be established by probabilities or possibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mere fact that something may result is insufficient. Examiners must look for evidence that the missing matter is necessarily present, not merely possible or probable (In re Robertson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete patentability determination and communication in Office actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel must complete the patentability determination under all relevant statutory provisions of title 35 (including 101, 112, 102, 103) and review proposed rejections and their bases to confirm correctness before imposing any rejection in an Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office action should clearly communicate findings, conclusions, and reasons which support them, and when possible offer helpful suggestions on how to overcome rejections. Examiners should not impose a written description rejection without considering other statutory requirements and the whole record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original claims and functional language risks
rubrics_metrics.description: An original claim may lack written description support when (1) it defines the invention in functional language specifying a desired result but the disclosure fails to sufficiently identify how the function is performed or the result is achieved, or (2) a broad genus claim is presented but the disclosure only describes a narrow species with no evidence the genus is contemplated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if claim language appears verbatim in the specification, mere indistinct words do not necessarily satisfy the requirement. Courts (e.g., Ariad) caution that appearance of language alone is not dispositive; the disclosure must enable recognition of possession.
